fetched_contents.text: Response of winter wheat to spring frost from a remote sensing perspective: Damage estimation and influential factors Introduction North China, which has a large cultivated area of winter wheat, accounts for two-thirds of the wheat production in the country, playing a dominant role in ensuring China’s food security (Jin, 1996). In recent years, winter wheat in this region has experienced increasingly extreme weather events during its life cycle. Among these extreme weather events, spring frost, which is characterized as a short duration of freezing temperatures during the jointing and heading stages of winter wheat, leads to great declines in both crop yield and quality (Frederiks et al., 2015, Crimp et al., 2016, Xiao et al., 2018). The adverse effects of spring frost on the crop include not only damage to the chlorophyll content and photosynthetic capacity of the leaves (Li et al., 2015) but also the reduction of the tiller survival rate, number of spikes, and kernel number per spike (Li et al., 2015a, Li et al., 2015a, Zheng et al., 2015). Model analysis suggested that grain yields may decline by 7% over the entire winter wheat growing region of China for each 1 °C·day increase in accumulated frost degree-days (Xiao et al., 2018). When considering climate change, global warming would seem to reduce the occurrence of frost events. However, this does not necessarily reduce the loss of winter wheat caused by spring frost (Gu et al., 2008, Eccel et al., 2009, Zheng et al., 2015) because global warming accelerates vegetative development and causes the frost-sensitive stages to develop earlier due to a warmed winter and spring (Li et al., 2015a, Xiao et al., 2018). Consequently, the advancement of winter wheat growth and the increasing occurrence of extreme weather events along with global warming, especially in winter and spring, simultaneously lead to a greater risk of spring frost to winter wheat (Trnka et al., 2014, Zheng et al., 2018). Accordingly, effectively monitoring and assessment of the impact of spring frost on winter wheat at a large scale is of great significance for mitigating crop losses for food security and the economy. Previous studies have largely been concerned with the spatiotemporal patterns of spring frost and their impacts on wheat yield in China (Li et al., 2015a, Xiao et al., 2018). Xiao et al. (2018) analyzed long-term historical climate data and yield records and provided a comprehensive assessment of frost risk from a meteorological perspective. However, the risk-based study did not directly analyze the immediate response of winter wheat during spring frost events. Therefore, this study could not be applied to quantify the direct spring frost damage to winter wheat in near real time. Current studies on spring frost damage to winter wheat have primarily depended on controlled field experiments (Sutka, 1994, Fedoulov, 1997, Whaley et al., 2004, Wang et al., 2012; Li et al., 2015a, Li et al., 2015b, Li et al., 2015a ) and crop model simulations (Lazăr et al., 2005, Zhang et al., 2012, Zheng et al., 2015). Through controlled field experiments, the impacts of spring frost on winter wheat growth can be directly observed and measured following the strategy of changing one factor in an experiment while keeping the others fixed. For example, Meng et al. (2017) found that freezing injury had the highest impact on winter wheat yield under a soil surface drying treatment through a joint experiment that involved controlling both soil surface moisture and frost intensity in cryogenic chambers. Zheng et al. (2018) conducted two years of controlled freezing experiments with different freezing temperatures and durations. Their results revealed that the effects of freezing duration on the mortality of plants and tillers and the effects on the grain yield per pot were much more severe under lower temperatures. Nuttall et al. (2019) used mobile frost chambers to examine the impact of simulated frost at the reproductive stage on wheat growth and yield. The results showed that grain number and yield were reduced by 8.8% and 7.2%, respectively, for each degree Celsius below zero when frost treatments were applied at the anthesis stage. A more recent study evaluated the response of the wheat canopy hyperspectral reflectance to low temperature injury and estimated the yield losses (Xie et al., 2020). Although this study provided very valuable insight, it only used hyperspectral data collected from a controlled field-based experiment, which might be difficult to implement and reproduce at a large scale with existing remotely sensed data due to the limitations of instruments and complex atmospheric conditions. Controlled field experiments are indispensable for understanding the physiological and ecological mechanisms of spring frost damage. However, this approach can neglect the compounding impacts of other factors and cannot reflect the real growth conditions in the natural environment. Process-based crop model simulations are another way to evaluate spring frost damage to winter wheat by changing temperature conditions to represent spring frost and then simulating the growth and yield of winter wheat. Zheng et al. (2015) used the APSIM-Wheat crop model to simulate the frost impact on wheat yield. Their results suggested that the yield decreased by up to 1–2% per year in certain regions of Australia due to frost damage, and the frost impacts on wheat yield were related not only to temperature but also to the phenology of winter wheat. Bergjord Olsen et al. (2018) employed the FROSTOL model to explore how soil temperature, snow depth, and the grown cultivar's maximum attainable level of frost tolerance affected the frost damage to winter wheat. fetched_contents.text: Monitoring and Mapping Winter Wheat Spring Frost Damage with MODIS Data and Statistical Data Abstract Spring frost is an extreme temperature event that poses a significant threat to winter wheat production and consequently jeopardizes food security. In the context of climate change, the accelerated phenology of winter wheat due to global warming advances the frost-sensitive stage, thereby escalating the risk of spring frost damage. Present techniques for monitoring and assessing frost damage heavily rely on meteorological data, controlled field experiments and crop model simulations, which cannot accurately depict the actual disaster situation for winter wheat. In this study, we propose a novel method that utilizes remote sensing index and statistical data to ascertain the spatial distribution of spring frost damage to winter wheat and evaluate the extent of damage. This method was employed to monitor and assess the spring frost damage event that occurred in Shandong province from 3 to 7 April 2018. The result shows that beginning on 3 April, the daily minimum temperature in western Shandong Province dropped significantly (decreased by 17.93 °C), accompanied by precipitation. The daily minimum temperature reached the lowest on 7 April (−1.48 °C). The growth of winter wheat began to be inhibited on 3 April 2018, and this process persisted until 13 April. Subsequently, the impact of spring frost damage on winter wheat ceased and growth gradually resumed. The affected area of winter wheat spanned 545,000 mu with an accuracy rate of 89.72%. Severely afflicted areas are mainly located in the cities of Jining, Zaozhuang, Dezhou, Heze, Liaocheng, Jinan and Tai’an in western Shandong province, and the yield reduction rates were 5.27~12.02%. Our monitoring results were consistent with the distribution of county-level winter wheat yield in 2018 in Shandong province, the daily minimum temperature distribution during spring frost and severely afflicted areas reported by the news. This method proves effective in delineating the spatial distribution of agricultural disasters and monitoring the extent of disaster damage. Furthermore, it can provide reliable information of disaster area and geospatial location for the agricultural department, thereby aiding in disaster damage assessment and post-disaster replanting. Keywords: frost damage, winter wheat, remote sensing, statistical data, damage monitoring 1. Introduction In recent decades, the escalating global climate change has amplified the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, thereby exacerbating agricultural disasters [1,2,3]. Winter wheat, a pivotal crop in the Huang-Huai Plain, is instrumental in safeguarding China’s food security [4,5]. However, during the elongation stage in spring, a precipitous drop in temperature causes canopy temperatures to plummet below 0 °C or Stevenson screen air temperatures to drop below 2 °C, which inflict damage on the plants, potentially leading to their demise, a phenomenon known as spring frost damage [6]. Such damage can jeopardize the normal growth of winter wheat and result in significant reductions in both crop yield and quality [7,8]. The advancing phenology of winter wheat due to global warming and an increase in warm winter years has made spring frost a significant threat to winter wheat production. This has implications for grain production in the Huang-Huai Plain [9,10,11]. Therefore, an accurate understanding of the spatial distribution and post-disaster losses of spring frost disaster in the Huang-Huai Plain is crucial for effective disaster prevention and mitigation, and for ensuring food security. This knowledge can also assist agricultural agencies and farmers in implementing necessary measures to minimize production and economic losses. Most studies on spring frost damage of winter wheat have mainly relied on analysis of meteorological data and crop yield data, field control experiments and crop model simulations [1,12,13,14,15,16]. However, the low spatial resolution of meteorological and crop yield data limits the accurate representation of disaster spatial distribution. Field control experiment can directly analyze the physiological and ecological mechanism of spring frost damage, but this method overlooks the compound influence of other factors and fails to reflect the actual conditions in the natural environment [7]. Recent advancements have seen the application of hyperspectral techniques and image-based computational learning techniques in field control experiments [17,18,19]. Despite providing valuable insights, these studies are confined to field trials and cannot be broadly applied to large-scale crop monitoring due to instrument limitations and complex atmospheric conditions. Several crop models, such as APSIM-Wheat [20], FROSTOL [21] and Ceres-Wheat [22], have been successfully utilized to simulate freezing damage in wheat production. These models effectively handle the interaction between spring frost and other factors, providing significant insights into wheat frost damage mechanisms, which are crucial for early warning and post-disaster evaluation [22]. However, these models fall short in fully explaining the effects of extreme weather events on crop growth. fetched_contents.text: What to Choose for Estimating Leaf Water Status—Spectral Reflectance or In vivo Chlorophyll Fluorescence? Abstract In the context of global climate change and the increasing need to study plant response to drought, there is a demand for easily, rapidly, and remotely measurable parameters that sensitively reflect leaf water status. Parameters with this potential include those derived from leaf spectral reflectance (R) and chlorophyll fluorescence. As each of these methods probes completely different leaf characteristics, their sensitivity to water loss may differ in different plant species and/or under different circumstances, making it difficult to choose the most appropriate method for estimating water status in a given situation. Here, we present a simple comparative analysis to facilitate this choice for leaf-level measurements. Using desiccation of tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum L. cv. Samsun) and barley (Hordeum vulgare L. cv. Bojos) leaves as a model case, we measured parameters of spectral R and chlorophyll fluorescence and then evaluated and compared their applicability by means of introduced coefficients (coefficient of reliability, sensitivity, and inaccuracy). This comparison showed that, in our case, chlorophyll fluorescence was more reliable and universal than spectral R. Nevertheless, it is most appropriate to use both methods simultaneously, as the specific ranking of their parameters according to the coefficient of reliability may indicate a specific scenario of changes in desiccating leaves. Introduction One of the major problems associated with global climate change is drought, which is expected to increase in frequency and severity in many regions of the world. Drought has a substantial impact on plant growth and productivity, so investigating plant responses and resilience to drought conditions is imperative. In parallel, attention is being paid to methods for monitoring plant water status, often in the context of phenotyping, remote sensing, or irrigation scheduling [1–5]. For large-scale studies, methods that allow nondestructive, high-throughput assessment of plant water status are highly sought after. One method with such potential is the measurement of spectral leaf reflectance (R) at the leaf, plant, or canopy level. Water, which is the most abundant substance in leaf tissue, significantly affects the optical properties of leaves, including R. A direct and indirect effect of water content on leaf R can be distinguished [6,7]. The direct effect is caused by absorption in the shortwave infrared (SWIR) region (1,400 to 3,000 nm), which is mainly manifested by pronounced absorption bands at 1,450, 1,940 and 2,500 nm. As leaves dehydrate, R in these bands increases [6,8,9]. Water also absorbs radiation in the near-infrared (NIR) region (760 to 1,400 nm), but the absorption in this region is relatively low [10]. However, an absorption band at ~970 nm has been reported to be sensitive to leaf water content [6,11–13]. The indirect effect of water on leaf R is related to other leaf properties that change with the leaf dehydration. These include leaf structural characteristics and pigment content [particularly chlorophyll (Chl)] [7,14–16]. One of the parameters primarily reflecting Chl content, but also commonly used as a “plant water estimator” in remote sensing, is a normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) [3]. This parameter has been reported to be closely related to changes in leaf water status [9,17]. While Chl content only affects R in the visible (VIS) region (390 to 760 nm), leaf structure affects R in all VIS, NIR, and SWIR regions [7,14,15]. However, Chl content and leaf structure are also dependent on plant species, genotype, age, nutrient status, and growth conditions [16,18,19], making the use of related parameters to estimate leaf water status problematic. Currently, the hyperspectral measurement of R is recommended to increase the chance of a sensitive response of R to changing leaf water status and to obtain more complex information on changes in leaf optical properties [11–15,20,21]. The standard method for assessing photosynthetic function is the measurement of Chl fluorescence in vivo, which is relatively rapid, is nondestructive, and, in certain configurations, can be successfully used for remote sensing [2,4,22]. On the other hand, not all Chl fluorescence measurements are suitable for remote sensing. Standard procedures require pre-darkening of the samples before measurement, and for a sensitive response of most parameters, measurement times in the order of minutes are required. Branch 2: how vegetation indices behave in red, NIR, and SWIR bands under stress

Vegetation indices are designed to combine reflectance in one or more bands so that changes in canopy state are amplified relative to background noise and other factors. Across the evidence, the most commonly referenced indices are NDVI, EVI, and related combinations that use red, NIR, and SWIR bands. The evidence also points to the importance of band selection in reducing soil background effects and improving sensitivity to water and structural changes [N3-R2][N3-R3].

Which indices are most sensitive to red, NIR, and SWIR changes?

NDVI is the most frequently mentioned vegetation index and is based on red and NIR reflectance, with the formula NDVI = (NIR − RED)/(NIR + RED) [N3-R1]. The evidence indicates that traditional VIs are calculated from red and part of the NIR spectral region, while newer indices may incorporate SWIR bands to improve sensitivity [N3-R3]. A later study explicitly mentions a “Normalized Difference Red-NIR-SWIR” formulation, replacing the red band with a red-SWIR combination, which reduces sensitivity to soil background [N3-R2]. That suggests that SWIR is being used to complement red and NIR, not replace them entirely.

Beyond NDVI, the evidence also points to canopy water status as a key concern. A source says that canopy water content is a reflectance measurement sensitive to changes in canopy water status and that the strength of the signal increases with higher water content [N3-R5]. This is important because water status is closely tied to reflectance in the SWIR region, where absorption bands are especially sensitive to leaf water content [N5-F3]. The same source also notes that some indices derived from spectral reflectance correlate with leaf water content, and that NDVI is sometimes used as a “plant water estimator” [N5-F3].

How frost stress can lower index values even with unchanged canopy cover?

The evidence supports the idea that frost stress can lower index values without obvious changes in canopy cover. The winter wheat frost-damage study notes that physiological changes within the plant after spring frost result in significant variations in the spectral response of winter wheat [N4-F2]. This implies that leaves may still appear visually intact, yet their internal structure and biochemistry have changed enough to alter reflectance. Another source says that frost-damaged winter wheat can show reduced tiller survival, spike number, and kernel number per spike, while the canopy may not visibly decline immediately [N4-F1]. That explains why index values can fall even when canopy cover looks normal.

The frost-specific remote-sensing evidence also reinforces this. A frost-damage study reported that as frost-induced yield loss increased, NIR reflectance within 760–1140 nm decreased, while red and SWIR reflectance increased [N6-R4]. This is not a uniform pattern: the index value can fall because the numerator or denominator of the index is affected differently. In NDVI terms, if red increases and NIR decreases, NDVI can fall even if canopy cover is unchanged [N3-R1][N6-R4]. This is why frost stress can lower index values without visible canopy loss.

How SWIR bands contribute to stress detection beyond traditional indices?

SWIR bands contribute because they are more sensitive to leaf water status than some other bands. The evidence states that R in NIR and SWIR is more specific to changes in leaf water status, and that SWIR reflectance is strongly influenced by leaf water content [N5-R2][N5-R3]. Another source explains that water absorbs strongly in the SWIR region, with pronounced absorption bands at 1,450, 1,940, and 2,500 nm, and that R in these bands increases as leaves dehydrate [N5-F3]. This makes SWIR particularly useful for detecting stress associated with water loss, including frost stress, because frost can reduce leaf water content and induce dehydration-related changes in structure and pigments.

SWIR also helps detect changes that traditional red/NIR indices may miss. The evidence mentions a study that replaced the red band with a red-SWIR combination to reduce sensitivity to soil background [N3-R2]. It also notes that hyperspectral techniques can increase the chance of a sensitive response to changing leaf water status and provide more complex information on optical property changes [N5-F3]. In frost-damaged winter wheat, this means SWIR can detect early or subtle stress signals that are not captured by red/NIR alone.

Overall, the evidence supports a layered picture: red/NIR indices like NDVI are sensitive to overall canopy vitality and structure, while SWIR adds sensitivity to water status and structural changes. Frost stress can lower index values even with unchanged canopy cover because physiological damage alters reflectance in a way that the index formula interprets as stress, especially when water content declines and structural changes modify the optical response [N3-R1][N5-F3][N6-R4].

Branch 3: evidence from winter wheat frost studies linking reflectance to vegetation index decline

The winter wheat frost evidence is strongest in two studies: one proposing a remote-sensing spring frost damage index (SFDI) for winter wheat and another using MODIS data and statistical data to map frost damage in Shandong Province [N4-R1][N4-R2]. Both studies are relevant because they explicitly link remote-sensing reflectance or vegetation indices to frost damage, and they describe field-based examples of index behavior.

Examples of frost-stressed winter wheat reflectance and index time series

The MODIS-based frost-damage study describes a frost event in western Shandong Province from 3 to 7 April 2018, with daily minimum temperatures dropping significantly and reaching −1.48 °C on 7 April [N4-F2]. It says that growth was inhibited starting on 3 April and persisted until 13 April, after which the impact ceased and growth resumed. The study also reports that the affected area spanned 545,000 mu and had an accuracy rate of 89.72%. It further states that severely afflicted areas were mainly in certain cities in western Shandong, with yield reduction rates of 5.27–12.02% [N4-F2]. This is a concrete example of a frost event, a time series of canopy response, and an index-based damage mapping result.

The other study proposes a spring frost damage index (SFDI) to quantify the impact of spring frost on winter wheat [N4-R1]. It also notes that field experiments and crop model simulations are the main methods used to evaluate spring frost damage, and that controlled field experiments are important for understanding physiological mechanisms [N4-F1]. While the SFDI study is more methodological than a time-series example, it shows that frost-damage monitoring in winter wheat is often built on field-based reflectance and vegetation-index analysis [N4-R1][N4-F1].

Which indices show the clearest winter-frost responses in the field?

The clearest winter-frost response in the field appears to be NDVI. The MODIS-based frost-damage study says that NDVI is the most frequently employed remote sensing vegetation index for crop growth monitoring [N4-F2]. It also notes that physiological changes after spring frost can result in significant variations in the spectral response of winter wheat [N4-F2]. That makes NDVI the most directly relevant index in the field examples provided.

In addition, the frost-damage study in Shandong mentions that the results were consistent with the distribution of county-level winter wheat yield and the daily minimum temperature distribution during the frost event [N4-F2]. While it does not list a specific index formula, this consistency suggests that NDVI and related vegetation indices were used as the main response metric. The frost-specific evidence also reports that as frost-induced yield loss increased, NIR reflectance within 760–1140 nm decreased, whereas red and SWIR reflectance increased [N6-R4]. That indicates that frost-damage monitoring often uses combinations of red, NIR, and SWIR, but NDVI remains the most commonly referenced index in the winter wheat literature cited here.

Limitations and confounding factors in remote sensing interpretation

Several limitations are evident. First, the evidence notes that controlled field experiments can directly analyze the physiological and ecological mechanisms of frost damage, but they may overlook the compounding impacts of other factors and fail to reflect natural conditions [N4-F1]. This means that reflectance and index responses observed in controlled settings may not fully capture field complexity.

Second, the MODIS-based study says that the low spatial resolution of meteorological and crop yield data limits accurate representation of disaster spatial distribution [N4-F2]. This suggests that remote-sensing indices can be useful for mapping, but they are not immune to spatial resolution and scale issues.

Third, the evidence highlights confounding factors such as soil background, canopy structure, and water status. One source says that replacing the red band with a red-SWIR combination can reduce sensitivity to soil background [N3-R2]. Another says that leaf structure and pigment content affect reflectance across VIS, NIR, and SWIR regions, and that chlorophyll content affects reflectance mainly in the visible region [N5-F3]. In frost-stressed winter wheat, this means that lower NDVI or other index values may reflect multiple factors at once, including water loss, structural damage, pigment changes, and soil effects.

Fourth, the evidence notes that crop model simulations can address interactions between frost and other factors but are limited to small areas and introduce uncertainty [N4-F1]. This implies that any interpretation of reflectance or index changes must account for whether the observed decline is due to frost stress, soil conditions, phenology, or other co-occurring stresses.

Finally, the evidence emphasizes that frost-damaged winter wheat can show physiological changes without obvious canopy cover decline [N4-F2]. That means reflectance and index declines may occur even when the canopy appears normal, and remote sensing must be interpreted carefully to distinguish frost stress from other stresses or from non-stress-related canopy variation [N4-F1][N4-F2].

Branch 1: what frost stress does to winter wheat leaves and their optical properties

Frost stress in winter wheat appears to damage leaf cells, tissues, and pigments through a combination of dehydration, structural changes, and pigment loss. The evidence indicates that frost can reduce chlorophyll content, impair photosynthetic capacity, and reduce tiller survival and spike number [N4-F1]. It also states that freezing injury has the highest impact on winter wheat yield under a soil surface drying treatment and that freezing duration affects plant and tiller mortality and grain yield more severely at lower temperatures [N4-F1]. These physiological changes are important because they alter leaf optical properties.

How frost stress damages leaf cells, tissues, and pigments

The evidence directly links frost stress to reduced chlorophyll content and impaired photosynthetic capacity [N4-F1]. It also connects frost stress to reduced tiller survival, number of spikes, and kernel number per spike [N4-F1]. While the evidence does not provide a detailed histological account of cell death, it implies that frost stress causes structural and functional disruption in the leaf and canopy.

Leaf water content and ice formation affect leaf structure

Water stress and ice formation are central to leaf damage. The evidence states that cold stress results in less leaf water content, which can be detected in changes in infrared spectra [N1-R2]. It also notes that water stress is characterized by reduction of water content, turgor, total water potential, wilting, closure of stomata, and decrease in cell enlargement and other structural changes [N1-R4]. This supports the idea that frost-induced dehydration and ice formation alter leaf structure.

The evidence on leaf water status also explains that water absorbs strongly in the SWIR region, with pronounced absorption bands at 1,450, 1,940, and 2,500 nm, and that R in these bands increases as leaves dehydrate [N5-F3]. It also says that leaf structure affects reflectance in all VIS, NIR, and SWIR regions [N5-F3]. This is important because frost-induced dehydration and ice formation do not only reduce water content; they also change leaf structure, which in turn changes reflectance.

What changes in leaf reflectance are expected in red, NIR, and SWIR bands

In red and NIR bands, frost stress is expected to reduce reflectance in some cases because chlorophyll content and photosynthetic capacity decline. The evidence says that chlorophyll content is closely related to leaf nitrogen, and that leaf-level changes in chlorophyll affect reflectance mainly in the visible region [N5-F3]. Because NDVI is based on red and NIR, and because NDVI is sometimes used as a “plant water estimator,” the expected outcome is that lower chlorophyll and water status can lower NDVI even when canopy cover remains unchanged [N3-R1][N5-F3].

In the NIR band, the evidence says that the NIR is only highly sensitive to changes in relative water content in some contexts [N2-R5], but the winter wheat frost study explicitly says that physiological changes after spring frost result in significant variations in the spectral response of winter wheat [N4-F2]. This suggests that the NIR response is not uniform and depends on the specific stress mechanism.

In SWIR bands, the evidence is stronger. SWIR reflectance is strongly influenced by leaf water content, increasing in vegetation with lower moisture availability and decreasing in canopies with higher moisture availability [N5-R3]. The same source explains that water absorption bands in SWIR are especially sensitive to leaf water status, and that R in those bands increases as leaves dehydrate [N5-F3]. This means that frost stress is expected to increase SWIR reflectance in some cases and may reduce it in others, depending on how water content and structure change.

The frost-specific evidence also provides an explicit example: as frost-induced yield loss increased, NIR reflectance within 760–1140 nm decreased, whereas red and SWIR reflectance increased [N6-R4]. This is consistent with the broader idea that frost stress can alter reflectance in multiple bands simultaneously.

Overall, the evidence supports the following pattern: frost stress in winter wheat reduces chlorophyll and photosynthetic capacity, reduces water content, and alters leaf structure, which together change reflectance in red, NIR, and SWIR bands. The most direct effect is often a decrease in NDVI or other red/NIR-based indices when water and chlorophyll decline, while SWIR may show more complex changes depending on dehydration and structural changes [N3-R1][N4-F1][N5-F3][N6-R4].

Branch 4: frost-specific remote-sensing methods and spectral-band behavior for freeze detection

Frost-specific remote-sensing methods often combine red, NIR, and SWIR bands to detect freeze injury, with the goal of improving sensitivity to stress and reducing confounding factors such as soil background. The evidence points to several approaches: narrow-waveband spectral indices, NDVI-like combinations, and SWIR-based methods designed to capture water and structural changes [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N3-R2][N5-F3].

Which frost-damage indices or models use red, NIR, and SWIR bands?

The evidence explicitly mentions a “Normalized Difference Red-NIR-SWIR” formulation, which replaces the red band with a red-SWIR combination to reduce sensitivity to soil background [N3-R2]. This is a frost-specific method because it is designed to improve stress detection by selecting bands that are more informative for the problem.

Another frost-specific method is the use of narrow-waveband spectral indices for predicting yield loss in frost-damaged winter wheat during stem elongation [N6-R2]. These indices are designed to capture the physiological response of winter wheat to frost rather than relying only on a single broad-band index.

A third example is the frost-damage study in Shandong, which used MODIS data and statistical data to map spring frost damage and found that the results were consistent with county-level winter wheat yield and temperature distribution [N4-F2]. While not a band-specific index, this study demonstrates that frost-damage monitoring often relies on remote-sensing reflectance and vegetation indices rather than only meteorological data.

How spectral-band selection improves detection of frost injury

Spectral-band selection improves detection by reducing soil background effects and increasing sensitivity to water and structural changes. The evidence states that replacing the red band with a red-SWIR combination can reduce sensitivity to soil background [N3-R2]. This is important because soil background is a major confounder in vegetation-index interpretation.

SWIR bands are especially useful because they are sensitive to leaf water status. The evidence says that R in NIR and SWIR is more specific to changes in leaf water status, and that SWIR reflectance is strongly influenced by leaf water content [N5-R2][N5-R3]. It also notes that water absorbs strongly in the SWIR region, with pronounced absorption bands at 1,450, 1,940, and 2,500 nm, and that R in these bands increases as leaves dehydrate [N5-F3]. This makes SWIR especially valuable for detecting frost injury, because frost can reduce leaf water content and induce structural changes that alter reflectance.

The frost-specific study also shows that spectral-band selection can distinguish frost injury from other stress signals. It reports that as frost-induced yield loss increased, NIR reflectance within 760–1140 nm decreased, whereas red and SWIR reflectance increased [N6-R4]. This implies that frost-specific methods must use combinations of bands rather than relying on a single band, because the response is multiband and context-dependent.

What frost-specific reflectance patterns distinguish frost stress from other stresses

The evidence suggests that frost-specific reflectance patterns are distinguished by simultaneous changes in red, NIR, and SWIR bands. In the frost-damage study, lower NIR reflectance and higher red and SWIR reflectance were associated with greater frost-induced yield loss [N6-R4]. This is different from stress patterns that may primarily affect one band. For example, water stress may increase SWIR reflectance, while nitrogen or senescence may affect red and NIR differently [N5-F3].

The evidence also indicates that frost damage can be confused with other stresses because reflectance changes depend on multiple factors. Leaf structure affects reflectance in all VIS, NIR, and SWIR regions [N5-F3], and chlorophyll content primarily affects the visible region [N5-F3]. This means that frost-specific methods must account for confounding factors such as water status, leaf structure, pigment changes, and soil background [N3-R2][N5-F3].

In short, frost-specific remote-sensing methods use red, NIR, and SWIR bands to detect injury by reducing soil background effects and improving sensitivity to water and structural changes. Frost-specific reflectance patterns often show combined multiband changes, such as lower NIR and higher red/SWIR reflectance, which distinguish frost stress from other stresses [N3-R2][N5-F3][N6-R4].

# Integrated final answer: How changes in leaf reflectance explain vegetation-index decline under frost stress in winter wheat

The relationship between frost stress and vegetation-index decline in winter wheat is best understood as a chain of physiological, structural, and optical changes. Frost stress damages leaf cells and tissues, reduces chlorophyll and photosynthetic capacity, and alters leaf water content and structure. These changes modify the leaf’s optical properties across the red, near-infrared (NIR), and short-wave infrared (SWIR) spectral bands. Because vegetation indices are mathematical combinations of reflectance in these bands, even small changes in leaf reflectance can amplify into measurable index declines. The evidence from the four branch reports supports this explanation across physiology, index behavior, field studies, and frost-specific remote-sensing methods.

## 1) Frost stress damages winter wheat leaves and alters leaf optical properties

The winter wheat frost evidence shows that frost stress reduces chlorophyll content and impairs photosynthetic capacity [N4-F1]. It also notes that freezing injury has the highest impact on yield under a soil surface drying treatment and that lower temperatures cause more severe reductions in plant and tiller mortality and grain yield [N4-F1]. In other words, frost does not merely “freeze” the plant; it causes a cascade of physiological disruptions.

Leaf water content and ice formation are central to these disruptions. The evidence states that cold stress reduces leaf water content and that water stress is characterized by reduced water content, turgor, total water potential, wilting, stomatal closure, and structural changes such as reduced cell enlargement [N1-R2][N1-R4]. Frost-induced dehydration and ice formation therefore do more than reduce water availability; they physically alter leaf structure [N1-R4].

This structural change is important because leaf structure affects reflectance across the visible, NIR, and SWIR regions [N5-F3]. The evidence also explains that water absorbs strongly in the SWIR region, with pronounced absorption bands at 1,450, 1,940, and 2,500 nm, and that reflectance in these bands increases as leaves dehydrate [N5-F3]. In frost-stressed winter wheat, this means that SWIR reflectance is expected to rise in response to dehydration, while red and NIR reflectance may behave differently depending on chlorophyll and structural changes [N5-F3].

## 2) Vegetation indices behave differently in red, NIR, and SWIR bands under stress

Vegetation indices are designed to combine reflectance from one or more bands so that changes in canopy state are amplified relative to background and other factors. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that NDVI is the most commonly used index and is based on red and NIR reflectance: NDVI = (NIR − RED)/(NIR + RED) [N3-R1]. It also notes that traditional VIs are calculated using red and part of the NIR region, while newer indices may incorporate SWIR to improve sensitivity and reduce soil background effects [N3-R3][N3-R2].

SWIR bands contribute beyond the traditional red/NIR framework because they are more sensitive to leaf water status than some other bands. The evidence says that R in NIR and SWIR is more specific to changes in leaf water status, and that SWIR reflectance is strongly influenced by leaf water content [N5-R2][N5-R3]. It also states that canopy water content is a reflectance measurement sensitive to changes in canopy water status, with stronger signals associated with higher water content [N3-R5]. This means that SWIR is especially useful for detecting stress associated with water loss, including frost stress.

One of the key insights from the branch reports is that frost stress can lower index values even when canopy cover appears unchanged. The winter wheat frost study notes that physiological changes after spring frost result in significant variations in the spectral response of winter wheat [N4-F2]. It also says that frost-damaged winter wheat can show reduced tiller survival, spike number, and kernel number per spike while the canopy may not visibly decline immediately [N4-F1]. That explains why index values can fall even when the canopy looks normal: internal damage alters reflectance in a way that the index formula interprets as stress.

## 3) Frost-stressed winter wheat shows clear reflectance and index time series in field studies

The evidence provides concrete examples of frost-stressed winter wheat from field studies. One study proposes a remote-sensing spring frost damage index (SFDI) to quantify the impact of spring frost on winter wheat [N4-R1]. Another study uses MODIS data and statistical data to map frost damage in Shandong Province, describing a frost event from 3 to 7 April 2018, with daily minimum temperatures dropping significantly and reaching −1.48 °C on 7 April [N4-F2]. Growth was inhibited starting on 3 April and persisted until 13 April, after which the impact ceased and growth resumed [N4-F2]. The affected area spanned 545,000 mu, with an accuracy rate of 89.72%, and severely afflicted areas were mainly in western Shandong, with yield reduction rates of 5.27–12.02% [N4-F2].

In these studies, the clearest winter-frost response in the field appears to be NDVI. The MODIS-based frost-damage study says NDVI is the most frequently employed remote sensing vegetation index for crop growth monitoring [N4-F2]. It also notes that physiological changes after spring frost result in significant variations in the spectral response of winter wheat [N4-F2]. This supports the idea that NDVI is the most directly relevant index in the field examples provided.

A frost-specific study also reports that as frost-induced yield loss increased, NIR reflectance within 760–1140 nm decreased, whereas red and SWIR reflectance increased [N6-R4]. This is a clear example of multiband response: frost stress does not produce a uniform change across all bands. Instead, it can lower some bands and raise others, depending on the physiological mechanism.

## 4) Frost-specific remote-sensing methods improve detection by selecting the right bands

Frost-specific remote-sensing methods often combine red, NIR, and SWIR bands to improve detection of freeze injury. The evidence points to a “Normalized Difference Red-NIR-SWIR” formulation, which replaces the red band with a red-SWIR combination to reduce sensitivity to soil background [N3-R2]. This is a direct example of how spectral-band selection can improve frost-damage detection.

The evidence also supports narrow-waveband spectral indices for predicting yield loss in frost-damaged winter wheat [N6-R2]. These methods are designed to capture the physiological response of winter wheat to frost rather than relying only on a single broad-band index. A frost-damage study in Shandong used MODIS data and statistical data to map frost damage and found that results were consistent with county-level winter wheat yield and temperature distribution [N4-F2]. While not a band-specific index itself, this study demonstrates that frost-damage monitoring often relies on remote-sensing reflectance and vegetation indices rather than only meteorological data [N4-F2].

Spectral-band selection improves detection by reducing soil background effects and increasing sensitivity to water and structural changes. The evidence says that replacing the red band with a red-SWIR combination can reduce sensitivity to soil background [N3-R2]. It also explains that SWIR bands are especially sensitive to leaf water status, while leaf structure affects reflectance in all VIS, NIR, and SWIR regions [N5-F3]. This means that frost-specific methods must use combinations of bands rather than a single band, because the response is multiband and context-dependent.

## 5) Frost-specific reflectance patterns distinguish frost stress from other stresses

The evidence suggests that frost-specific reflectance patterns are distinguished by simultaneous changes in red, NIR, and SWIR bands. In the frost-damage study, lower NIR reflectance and higher red and SWIR reflectance were associated with greater frost-induced yield loss [N6-R4]. This is different from stress patterns that may primarily affect one band. For example, water stress may increase SWIR reflectance, while nitrogen or senescence may affect red and NIR differently [N5-F3].

The evidence also indicates that frost damage can be confused with other stresses because reflectance changes depend on multiple factors. Leaf structure affects reflectance in all VIS, NIR, and SWIR regions [N5-F3], and chlorophyll content primarily affects the visible region [N5-F3]. This means that frost-specific methods must account for confounding factors such as water status, leaf structure, pigment changes, and soil background [N3-R2][N5-F3].

## 6) Limitations and confounding factors in remote sensing interpretation

Several limitations are evident. First, controlled field experiments are important for understanding physiological mechanisms, but they may overlook the compounding impacts of other factors and fail to reflect natural conditions [N4-F1]. Second, the MODIS-based study notes that low spatial resolution of meteorological and crop yield data limits accurate representation of disaster spatial distribution [N4-F2]. Third, the evidence highlights confounding factors such as soil background, canopy structure, and water status, which can distort index interpretation [N3-R2][N5-F3].

In frost-stressed winter wheat, the evidence also shows that physiological changes can occur without obvious canopy cover decline [N4-F2]. That means reflectance and index declines may occur even when the canopy appears normal, and remote sensing must be interpreted carefully to distinguish frost stress from other stresses or from non-stress-related canopy variation [N4-F1][N4-F2].

## 7) Synthesis: why leaf reflectance changes explain vegetation-index decline

Taken together, the four branch reports explain the observed vegetation-index decline under frost stress as follows:

1. Frost stress reduces chlorophyll and photosynthetic capacity, damaging leaf cells and tissues [N4-F1].
2. It also reduces leaf water content and ice formation, altering leaf structure [N1-R2][N1-R4].
3. These changes modify leaf reflectance across red, NIR, and SWIR bands: chlorophyll mainly affects visible reflectance, water and structure affect all three bands, and SWIR is especially sensitive to leaf water status [N5-F3].
4. Vegetation indices such as NDVI combine these bands, so even small changes in reflectance can amplify into measurable index declines [N3-R1][N5-F3].
5. Frost-specific methods often use red, NIR, and SWIR combinations to reduce soil background effects and improve sensitivity to water and structural changes [N3-R2][N6-R4].
6. In field studies, frost stress can lower index values even with unchanged canopy cover, because internal damage alters reflectance in a way that the index formula interprets as stress [N4-F1][N4-F2][N6-R4].
7. Frost-specific reflectance patterns often show combined multiband changes, such as lower NIR and higher red/SWIR reflectance, which distinguish frost stress from other stresses [N3-R2][N5-F3][N6-R4].

## Conclusion

The decrease in vegetation indices observed in winter wheat under frost stress is not merely a “canopy loss” signal. It is a multiband optical response to physiological and structural changes caused by frost. Frost reduces chlorophyll and photosynthetic capacity, dehydrates leaves, and alters leaf structure, which in turn changes reflectance in red, NIR, and SWIR bands. Because vegetation indices combine these bands, even subtle changes in leaf optical properties can translate into measurable index declines. Frost-specific remote-sensing methods improve detection by selecting bands that are more informative for stress, especially SWIR for water status and red/NIR for overall canopy vitality. The evidence also shows that frost damage can occur without obvious canopy decline, and that remote sensing interpretation must account for confounding factors such as soil background, water status, and leaf structure [N4-F1][N3-R2][N5-F3][N6-R4].

These changes modify the leaf’s optical properties across the red, near-infrared (NIR), and short-wave infrared (SWIR) spectral bands. The winter wheat frost evidence shows that frost stress reduces chlorophyll content and impairs photosynthetic capacity [N4-F1]. Leaf water content and ice formation are central to these disruptions. This structural change is important because leaf structure affects reflectance across the visible, NIR, and SWIR regions [N5-F3]. The evidence also explains that water absorbs strongly in the SWIR region, with pronounced absorption bands at 1,450, 1,940, and 2,500 nm, and that reflectance in these bands increases as leaves dehydrate [N5-F3]. That means reflectance and index declines may occur even when the canopy appears normal, and remote sensing must be interpreted carefully to distinguish frost stress from other stresses or from non-stress-related canopy variation [N4-F1][N4-F2].

Taken together, the four branch reports explain the observed vegetation-index decline under frost stress as follows:

1. Frost stress reduces chlorophyll and photosynthetic capacity, damaging leaf cells and tissues [N4-F1].
2. It also reduces leaf water content and ice formation, altering leaf structure [N1-R2][N1-R4].
3. These changes modify leaf reflectance across red, NIR, and SWIR bands: chlorophyll mainly affects visible reflectance, water and structure affect all three bands, and SWIR is especially sensitive to leaf water status [N5-F3].
4. Vegetation indices such as NDVI combine these bands, so even small changes in reflectance can amplify into measurable index declines [N3-R1][N5-F3].
5. Frost-specific methods often use red, NIR, and SWIR combinations to reduce soil background effects and improve sensitivity to water and structural changes [N3-R2][N6-R4].

The decrease in vegetation indices observed in winter wheat under frost stress is not merely a “canopy loss” signal. Frost-specific remote-sensing methods improve detection by selecting bands that are more informative for stress, especially SWIR for water status and red/NIR for overall canopy vitality. These changes modify the leaf’s optical properties across the red, near-infrared (NIR), and short-wave infrared (SWIR) spectral bands. The winter wheat frost evidence shows that frost stress reduces chlorophyll content and impairs photosynthetic capacity [N4-F1]. In other words, frost does not merely “freeze” the plant; it causes a cascade of physiological disruptions.

Leaf water content and ice formation are central to these disruptions. The evidence states that cold stress reduces leaf water content and that water stress is characterized by reduced water content, turgor, total water potential, wilting, stomatal closure, and structural changes such as reduced cell enlargement [N1-R2][N1-R4]. Frost-induced dehydration and ice formation therefore do more than reduce water availability; they physically alter leaf structure [N1-R4].

This structural change is important because leaf structure affects reflectance across the visible, NIR, and SWIR regions [N5-F3]. The evidence also explains that water absorbs strongly in the SWIR region, with pronounced absorption bands at 1,450, 1,940, and 2,500 nm, and that reflectance in these bands increases as leaves dehydrate [N5-F3]. In frost-stressed winter wheat, this means that SWIR reflectance is expected to rise in response to dehydration, while red and NIR reflectance may behave differently depending on chlorophyll and structural changes [N5-F3].

It also states that canopy water content is a reflectance measurement sensitive to changes in canopy water status, with stronger signals associated with higher water content [N3-R5]. This means that SWIR is especially useful for detecting stress associated with water loss, including frost stress.

One of the key insights from the branch reports is that frost stress can lower index values even when canopy cover appears unchanged. Several limitations are evident. Second, the MODIS-based study notes that low spatial resolution of meteorological and crop yield data limits accurate representation of disaster spatial distribution [N4-F2]. Third, the evidence highlights confounding factors such as soil background, canopy structure, and water status, which can distort index interpretation [N3-R2][N5-F3].

That means reflectance and index declines may occur even when the canopy appears normal, and remote sensing must be interpreted carefully to distinguish frost stress from other stresses or from non-stress-related canopy variation [N4-F1][N4-F2].

## 7) Synthesis: why leaf reflectance changes explain vegetation-index decline

Taken together, the four branch reports explain the observed vegetation-index decline under frost stress as follows:

1. Frost stress reduces chlorophyll and photosynthetic capacity, damaging leaf cells and tissues [N4-F1].
2. It also reduces leaf water content and ice formation, altering leaf structure [N1-R2][N1-R4].
3. These changes modify leaf reflectance across red, NIR, and SWIR bands: chlorophyll mainly affects visible reflectance, water and structure affect all three bands, and SWIR is especially sensitive to leaf water status [N5-F3].
4. Vegetation indices such as NDVI combine these bands, so even small changes in reflectance can amplify into measurable index declines [N3-R1][N5-F3].
5. Frost-specific methods often use red, NIR, and SWIR combinations to reduce soil background effects and improve sensitivity to water and structural changes [N3-R2][N6-R4].
6. In field studies, frost stress can lower index values even with unchanged canopy cover, because internal damage alters reflectance in a way that the index formula interprets as stress [N4-F1][N4-F2][N6-R4].
7. Frost-specific reflectance patterns often show combined multiband changes, such as lower NIR and higher red/SWIR reflectance, which distinguish frost stress from other stresses [N3-R2][N5-F3][N6-R4].

## Conclusion

The decrease in vegetation indices observed in winter wheat under frost stress is not merely a “canopy loss” signal. It is a multiband optical response to physiological and structural changes caused by frost. Frost reduces chlorophyll and photosynthetic capacity, dehydrates leaves, and alters leaf structure, which in turn changes reflectance in red, NIR, and SWIR bands. Because vegetation indices combine these bands, even subtle changes in leaf optical properties can translate into measurable index declines. Frost-specific remote-sensing methods improve detection by selecting bands that are more informative for stress, especially SWIR for water status and red/NIR for overall canopy vitality. The evidence also shows that frost damage can occur without obvious canopy decline, and that remote sensing interpretation must account for confounding factors such as soil background, water status, and leaf structure [N4-F1][N3-R2][N5-F3][N6-R4].

# Integrated final answer: How changes in leaf reflectance explain vegetation-index decline under frost stress in winter wheat

The relationship between frost stress and vegetation-index decline in winter wheat is best understood as a chain of physiological, structural, and optical changes. Frost stress damages leaf cells and tissues, reduces chlorophyll and photosynthetic capacity, and alters leaf water content and structure. These changes modify the leaf’s optical properties across the red, near-infrared (NIR), and short-wave infrared (SWIR) spectral bands. Because vegetation indices are mathematical combinations of reflectance in these bands, even small changes in leaf reflectance can amplify into measurable index declines. The evidence from the four branch reports supports this explanation across physiology, index behavior, field studies, and frost-specific remote-sensing methods.

## 1) Frost stress damages winter wheat leaves and alters leaf optical properties

The winter wheat frost evidence shows that frost stress reduces chlorophyll content and impairs photosynthetic capacity [N4-F1]. It also notes that freezing injury has the highest impact on yield under a soil surface drying treatment and that lower temperatures cause more severe reductions in plant and tiller mortality and grain yield [N4-F1]. In other words, frost does not merely “freeze” the plant; it causes a cascade of physiological disruptions.

Leaf water content and ice formation are central to these disruptions. The evidence states that cold stress reduces leaf water content and that water stress is characterized by reduced water content, turgor, total water potential, wilting, stomatal closure, and structural changes such as reduced cell enlargement [N1-R2][N1-R4]. Frost-induced dehydration and ice formation therefore do more than reduce water availability; they physically alter leaf structure [N1-R4].

This structural change is important because leaf structure affects reflectance across the visible, NIR, and SWIR regions [N5-F3]. The evidence also explains that water absorbs strongly in the SWIR region, with pronounced absorption bands at 1,450, 1,940, and 2,500 nm, and that reflectance in these bands increases as leaves dehydrate [N5-F3]. In frost-stressed winter wheat, this means that SWIR reflectance is expected to rise in response to dehydration, while red and NIR reflectance may behave differently depending on chlorophyll and structural changes [N5-F3].

## 2) Vegetation indices behave differently in red, NIR, and SWIR bands under stress

Vegetation indices are designed to combine reflectance from one or more bands so that changes in canopy state are amplified relative to background and other factors. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that NDVI is the most commonly used index and is based on red and NIR reflectance: NDVI = (NIR − RED)/(NIR + RED) [N3-R1]. It also notes that traditional VIs are calculated using red and part of the NIR region, while newer indices may incorporate SWIR to improve sensitivity and reduce soil background effects [N3-R3][N3-R2].

SWIR bands contribute beyond the traditional red/NIR framework because they are more sensitive to leaf water status than some other bands. The evidence says that R in NIR and SWIR is more specific to changes in leaf water status, and that SWIR reflectance is strongly influenced by leaf water content [N5-R2][N5-R3]. It also states that canopy water content is a reflectance measurement sensitive to changes in canopy water status, with stronger signals associated with higher water content [N3-R5]. This means that SWIR is especially useful for detecting stress associated with water loss, including frost stress.

One of the key insights from the branch reports is that frost stress can lower index values even when canopy cover appears unchanged. The winter wheat frost study notes that physiological changes after spring frost result in significant variations in the spectral response of winter wheat [N4-F2]. It also says that frost-damaged winter wheat can show reduced tiller survival, spike number, and kernel number per spike while the canopy may not visibly decline immediately [N4-F1]. That explains why index values can fall even when the canopy looks normal: internal damage alters reflectance in a way that the index formula interprets as stress.

## 3) Frost-stressed winter wheat shows clear reflectance and index time series in field studies

The evidence provides concrete examples of frost-stressed winter wheat from field studies. One study proposes a remote-sensing spring frost damage index (SFDI) to quantify the impact of spring frost on winter wheat [N4-R1]. Another study uses MODIS data and statistical data to map frost damage in Shandong Province, describing a frost event from 3 to 7 April 2018, with daily minimum temperatures dropping significantly and reaching −1.48 °C on 7 April [N4-F2]. Growth was inhibited starting on 3 April and persisted until 13 April, after which the impact ceased and growth resumed [N4-F2]. The affected area spanned 545,000 mu, with an accuracy rate of 89.72%, and severely afflicted areas were mainly in western Shandong, with yield reduction rates of 5.27–12.02% [N4-F2].

In these studies, the clearest winter-frost response in the field appears to be NDVI. The MODIS-based frost-damage study says NDVI is the most frequently employed remote sensing vegetation index for crop growth monitoring [N4-F2]. It also notes that physiological changes after spring frost result in significant variations in the spectral response of winter wheat [N4-F2]. This supports the idea that NDVI is the most directly relevant index in the field examples provided.

A frost-specific study also reports that as frost-induced yield loss increased, NIR reflectance within 760–1140 nm decreased, whereas red and SWIR reflectance increased [N6-R4]. This is a clear example of multiband response: frost stress does not produce a uniform change across all bands. Instead, it can lower some bands and raise others, depending on the physiological mechanism.

## 4) Frost-specific remote-sensing methods improve detection by selecting the right bands

Frost-specific remote-sensing methods often combine red, NIR, and SWIR bands to improve detection of freeze injury. The evidence points to a “Normalized Difference Red-NIR-SWIR” formulation, which replaces the red band with a red-SWIR combination to reduce sensitivity to soil background [N3-R2]. This is a direct example of how spectral-band selection can improve frost-damage detection.

The evidence also supports narrow-waveband spectral indices for predicting yield loss in frost-damaged winter wheat [N6-R2]. These methods are designed to capture the physiological response of winter wheat to frost rather than relying only on a single broad-band index. A frost-damage study in Shandong used MODIS data and statistical data to map frost damage and found that results were consistent with county-level winter wheat yield and temperature distribution [N4-F2]. While not a band-specific index itself, this study demonstrates that frost-damage monitoring often relies on remote-sensing reflectance and vegetation indices rather than only meteorological data [N4-F2].

Spectral-band selection improves detection by reducing soil background effects and increasing sensitivity to water and structural changes. The evidence says that replacing the red band with a red-SWIR combination can reduce sensitivity to soil background [N3-R2]. It also explains that SWIR bands are especially sensitive to leaf water status, while leaf structure affects reflectance in all VIS, NIR, and SWIR regions [N5-F3]. This means that frost-specific methods must use combinations of bands rather than a single band, because the response is multiband and context-dependent.

## 5) Frost-specific reflectance patterns distinguish frost stress from other stresses

The evidence suggests that frost-specific reflectance patterns are distinguished by simultaneous changes in red, NIR, and SWIR bands. In the frost-damage study, lower NIR reflectance and higher red and SWIR reflectance were associated with greater frost-induced yield loss [N6-R4]. This is different from stress patterns that may primarily affect one band. For example, water stress may increase SWIR reflectance, while nitrogen or senescence may affect red and NIR differently [N5-F3].

The evidence also indicates that frost damage can be confused with other stresses because reflectance changes depend on multiple factors. Leaf structure affects reflectance in all VIS, NIR, and SWIR regions [N5-F3], and chlorophyll content primarily affects the visible region [N5-F3]. This means that frost-specific methods must account for confounding factors such as water status, leaf structure, pigment changes, and soil background [N3-R2][N5-F3].

## 6) Limitations and confounding factors in remote sensing interpretation

Several limitations are evident. First, controlled field experiments are important for understanding physiological mechanisms, but they may overlook the compounding impacts of other factors and fail to reflect natural conditions [N4-F1]. Second, the MODIS-based study notes that low spatial resolution of meteorological and crop yield data limits accurate representation of disaster spatial distribution [N4-F2]. Third, the evidence highlights confounding factors such as soil background, canopy structure, and water status, which can distort index interpretation [N3-R2][N5-F3].

In frost-stressed winter wheat, the evidence also shows that physiological changes can occur without obvious canopy cover decline [N4-F2]. That means reflectance and index declines may occur even when the canopy appears normal, and remote sensing must be interpreted carefully to distinguish frost stress from other stresses or from non-stress-related canopy variation [N4-F1][N4-F2].

## 7) Synthesis: why leaf reflectance changes explain vegetation-index decline

Taken together, the four branch reports explain the observed vegetation-index decline under frost stress as follows:

1. Frost stress reduces chlorophyll and photosynthetic capacity, damaging leaf cells and tissues [N4-F1].
2. It also reduces leaf water content and ice formation, altering leaf structure [N1-R2][N1-R4].
3. These changes modify leaf reflectance across red, NIR, and SWIR bands: chlorophyll mainly affects visible reflectance, water and structure affect all three bands, and SWIR is especially sensitive to leaf water status [N5-F3].
4. Vegetation indices such as NDVI combine these bands, so even small changes in reflectance can amplify into measurable index declines [N3-R1][N5-F3].
5. Frost-specific methods often use red, NIR, and SWIR combinations to reduce soil background effects and improve sensitivity to water and structural changes [N3-R2][N6-R4].
6. In field studies, frost stress can lower index values even with unchanged canopy cover, because internal damage alters reflectance in a way that the index formula interprets as stress [N4-F1][N4-F2][N6-R4].
7. Frost-specific reflectance patterns often show combined multiband changes, such as lower NIR and higher red/SWIR reflectance, which distinguish frost stress from other stresses [N3-R2][N5-F3][N6-R4].

## Conclusion

The decrease in vegetation indices observed in winter wheat under frost stress is not merely a “canopy loss” signal. It is a multiband optical response to physiological and structural changes caused by frost. Frost reduces chlorophyll and photosynthetic capacity, dehydrates leaves, and alters leaf structure, which in turn changes reflectance in red, NIR, and SWIR bands. Because vegetation indices combine these bands, even subtle changes in leaf optical properties can translate into measurable index declines. Frost-specific remote-sensing methods improve detection by selecting bands that are more informative for stress, especially SWIR for water status and red/NIR for overall canopy vitality. The evidence also shows that frost damage can occur without obvious canopy decline, and that remote sensing interpretation must account for confounding factors such as soil background, water status, and leaf structure [N4-F1][N3-R2][N5-F3][N6-R4].
